People did a lot of cocaine to this song, but it doesn’t sound like cocaine. It sounds natural and compassionate and connected: piano-gushes; a warm rush of strings; breathy, confiding vocals. The message is uncompromising: Get out on the dance floor, because the Protestant work ethic will kill you. But the delivery is generous, luxurious, streaming with a kind of angelic sanity. Formally, this song represents the perfection of dance music as played by humans. After this, more or less, it was over to the machines. The kick drum hits all four beats in the bar, and so does the bass. But these are master musicians, not synthesizers, so they can bend the rhythmic grid; they can warp it with their bodily presence; they can push, or inject a sweet, subliminal lag to which other bodily presences—especially those in disco pants—immediately respond; they can create a groove. And in America, the great groove is always militant: It sets you against society. Melody is good to me! Is there a lovelier battle cry than that?

Two voices, two Nickis. The first is lush and rueful, the voice of a torch singer still lingeringly high on the chemicals of romantic love, or refusing to come down; the second is that of a hitmaking rapper, sardonic and poised, with too many hangers-on, too many sycophants, too many bloodsuckers (including perhaps, the object of her love). Two forms of attachment. We’re overdosin’, sings the first voice, dreamy with desire, delivering itself to annihilation. The second voice is flatly managing its own fury and disappointment, and its refusal to be drained by parasites: Still don’t wish death on ’em / I just reflect on ’em. Success in America: It’s not for the faint of heart.

The candy mountains of this song are a particularly American kind of fantasy: the idyll of an early 20th-century hobo, a gentleman of the road who’s keenly feeling his predicament. So rich and fantastic is this reverie—free money growing on bushes, hens laying soft-boiled eggs—that we learn exactly what isn’t there, exactly what the singer has not got, exactly what he needs. And his needs are so basic! It’s not nirvana he’s looking for: He wants food and booze and cigarettes, and a change of socks.

McClintock had been a union organizer in the Texas oil fields, and a campaigner for the Industrial Workers of the World—the Wobblies—so he knew what he was singing about. In his hobo wonderland, for example, there is a magical absence of short-handled shovels (much used by chain gangs), and the railroad bulls, sworn enemy of the boxcar-jumping hoboes, are helpfully blind. Best of all, it’s a life without consequences: In the Big Rock Candy Mountains / The jails are made of tin / And you can walk right out again / As soon as you are in.

Longing

Hearing this song over the PA at CVS, its bellowed affirmations—Baby you’re a FIII-YA-WURK!—thinned to a Muzak crackle while you’re standing in line to pick up your tube of special ointment. Now that’s an American experience.

It was that faulty firework Russell Brand, Katy Perry’s then-husband, who directed her to the famous line in Jack Kerouac’s On the Road: the one about the people who “burn, burn, burn like fabulous yellow roman candles.” Or like proto–pop stars. So with the songwriter Ester Dean, and the Norwegian production duo Stargate, she wrote a mighty manifesto and a total banger. Her voice, wheedling through the downbeat verses—Do you ever feel like a plastic bag / drifting through the wind, wanting to start again?—rather exposed amid the spongy Stargate chords, swells to a superhuman enormity in the chorus.

Hey, Jack Kerouac, how was this for you? To see your delicate Beat gospel retooled as a city-crushing robo-saurus of a hit single—how did it make you feel? Like a plastic bag?

Not everyone liked Billie’s version of this song. The great New Yorker jazz writer Whitney Balliett pronounced it “depressing.” The BBC wouldn’t play it, on the grounds that it was detrimental to wartime morale. Also known as the “Hungarian Suicide Song,” “Gloomy Sunday” was composed in 1933 by Rezső Seress, a pianist from Budapest—who, 35 years later, indeed committed suicide. So here, in a clarinet-laden arrangement, we have lethal slow-acting Mitteleuropean doldrums coming up against … Billie Holiday: the narrow brassy purity of her note; her vibrato, like little throbs of life diffusing into a waste; her wised-up, witty, witchy way of sliding around the beat; and, above all (or below all), her sublime American fatalism, which is its own style, a kind of dark drollery—the flip side of American zeal.

Here, carried on the brute wave of Johnny’s guitar tone, is a tale of alienation, a Dostoyevskian skit—if Dostoyevsky was from Queens, New York. I heard about the Easter bunny / Presents under a Christmas tree / It was juvenile fantasy / There was no Mom or Daddy. Societally, this was the function of the Ramones: They made nursery rhymes for people who never had a nursery. (Or who, if they had one, burned it down.) With this song, the Ramones are moving fast. Their brand—an ultra-American mash-up of street gang, minor corporation, and feral family unit—is intensifying, as is their playing. In the compacted chords of the main riff, you can hear hardcore punk rock being born. Growing up, our narrator perilously enters society: He must interface with the job market. Knew I was ready for it / Some kind of employment. Brilliant writing: the off-kilter hauteur of the truly estranged. Obviously it’s never going to work out. So what can he do but rob a supermarket?

Taxi dancers, they were known as: hostesses renting themselves out as dance partners, one song at a time. Brittle gaiety was the mood, with an undertow of darkest misery. Or at least that’s the push-me-pull-you vibe of this song: The creaky little band strains against the slowed-down tempo—with one manic, foxtrotting outbreak—and Ruth Etting sings like a fast-talking movie dame who’s been drugged by melancholia. Seven to midnight I hear drums. She’s in musical hell. Shift over, she retires to her chilly hall room: quintessence of American loneliness. And there’s an answering American loneliness in her clientele, the men who pay for a dance; men adrift, unattended; her chorus of elderly beaus. Body warmth for sale.

A spiritual catastrophe has occurred. That’s what this song is about. Not that you’d know it from Ella Fitzgerald’s version, or Nat King Cole’s, or even droopy James Taylor’s—each of which is either too lush or too jaunty or too suave to touch the reality of the problem. And the problem is this: The world has been drained of meaning. It has become depthless, a kind of absurdist stage set, a canvas sky and a cardboard sea. So it falls to Cliff Edwards, vintage vaudevillian (he’s the voice of Jiminy Cricket in Disney’s Pinocchio), to convey the mood—the seeing-through of American illusion. It’s a Barnum and Bailey world / Just as phony as it can be. Edwards sounds almost nihilistically airy, like there’s no one else around, like he’s singing to himself, tickling his tiny ukelele, rooty-toot-tootling on an American streetcorner where everything has changed while looking exactly the same.

Loving this song gives me a nice lick of perversity, because the songwriters themselves notoriously don’t love it. In 1984, having delivered its second album—and first masterpiece—Ride the Lightning, Metallica finds itself under record-company pressure to add one more track, and to make it hit-like. A single, maybe. What the group comes up with is “Escape”: mid-paced, mega-chorused, written at speed in the studio. It wasn’t a hit. It wasn’t even a single. And it left the band unthrilled: In the 42 years since its release, its authors have performed it live precisely once. But “Escape” is a great Metallica song. The playing, and particularly James Hetfield’s rhythm-guitar work, guarantees its seriousness. Out for my own, out to be free / One with my mind, they just can’t see. Is this a statement of austere individualism, chiseled by the winds of time? Or is it pure, mutinous boneheadedness? Either way, American as hell.

Individuation: the American’s highest calling. But becoming yourself is a lonely business, by definition. Through levels of private wrongness you rise, through stages of almost esoteric discomfiture. If you’re lucky, you’ll recognize the initiatory moments for what they are. If you’re not, and you miss them, the change could bypass you altogether. Laura Jane Grace, the lead singer of Against Me!, is trans, and “Drinking With the Jocks” records a kind of botched initiation: an attempt to join the wrong tribe. Ritualized boozing and misogynist bluster. Horrible, violent laughter. If I do that, if I behave like that, will the jocks like me? The lyrics are brutal. This is an epic statement of injury—All of my life! All of my life!—delivered at high speed and with severe instrumental density. It’s what punk rock was invented for.

This one’s for the runaways. For the young Americans packing one bag and taking off, shaking the dust from their feet. It builds through a sequence of beginnings: a sharp tattoo of snare drum, an adrenalized bass line, a mind-clearing chord, and then a full-band detonation. Zen Arcade, of which this is the opener, is a double album, a Who-like creative sprawl. And it has a concept. It tells a story: young person runs away from home; takes to the road; is challenged, instructed, seduced, and finally overwhelmed by the merciless psychedelia of reality. The music is hardcore punk rock, furiously compacted and accelerated, but with mini-flourishes of pop classicism—a glancing vocal harmony, a chiming Byrdsy outro—that seem to trigger the enormity of the dream-space, of the unattainable American horizon.

The first gangsta-rap track? Could be. P.S.K. refers to a Philadelphia gang, the Parkside Killers, and Schoolly D’s wild-night narrative is a criminal picaresque: drugs, guns, prostitution, all of that. He raps in dissociated singsong, each line descending in pitch, downwardly curving like a sneer or an arc of desensitization. Groundbreaking stuff, at the time.

The rapping was one thing, but then there was the icy futurism of the beat. Programmed on a Roland TR-909 drum machine, it’s a masterpiece: an almighty synthetic crash, an emptiness shot through with spasms of mechanized rhythm, a hanging second of supercharged silence—repeat. Second, what they did to the beat. Finding themselves very high in a studio that contained a plate reverb—a refrigerator-size unit containing a sheet of stretched steel, built by the pre-digital American masters of echo and space to tingle, resound, deepen the wave—Schoolly and his associates went to town. “All of a sudden,” he told Philadelphia City Paper in 2004, “the song just took on this whole other life because we were just so fucked up. It just made this sucking sound like ‘boosh, boosh’ and we just looked at each other and were like, ‘Yeah, do more of that shit.’”

Some of the spaces—sonic and verbal—opened up by this song would soon be occupied. Ice-T and Eazy-E were attending closely to Schoolly’s hardcore flow, and the cymbal sounds of the 909 would find their way into Chicago house music. But that mystical, bass-y boosh, boosh—that came out of nowhere, went back into nowhere: an American anomaly, untouched by time.

There’s musicological interest here: Sara Carter’s voice, on this song, was one of the first recorded female lead vocals in country music, and her sister-in-law Maybelle Carter’s guitar technique—the famous “Carter scratch,” in which the melody twangs cleanly while the rhythm is scuffed out behind—was a stylistic breakthrough.

But that’s not why we listen to “Wildwood Flower.” The music of the Carter Family, reaching out to us from the area in the mountains of northeast Tennessee and southwest Virginia known as Poor Valley, is archetypal stoical American understatement, of the sort that Ernest Hemingway would have appreciated. “The dignity of movement of an iceberg,” he wrote in Death in the Afternoon, “is due to only one-eighth of it being above water.”

Late-period Hole. Courtney Love and her band have already left their red, red mark on the culture with 1994’s Live Through This, a howling fem-storm released the week after her husband, Kurt Cobain, killed himself. Love, by this point, has become a volatile celebrity. And now, with her band, she is seeking something very American: absolution via the mainstream. A remission from your own craziness, measured in records sold.

So with the producer/sonic hygienist Michael Beinhorn, they smooth it out. They shed the crusty vestments of grunge and go SoCal: Love still dominates, she’s still at the center of the mix with her slouchy-snarly, melody-smearing, poetry-uttering, big-mouth, punk-rock voice, but the cleaned-up band now pumps along in a nice Fleetwood Mac groove.

It works. It’s a hit. And it’s beautiful. The song is addressed to someone who’s right on the line, or perhaps already over it: either being reborn or self-incinerating. And Malibu is the magic word—the dreamy shoreline, America’s dissolution, waves leveling waves in the sunset while all of the red-hot sins of whoever you are sink hissing into the Pacific.

Rebellion

Musically, GNR always felt worn-out to me, sort of a jaded, late-stage confection: stale riffage, reheated rock-and-roll moves. But the anger, the shortwave wrath of Axl Rose, that was real. That was vivid. “To hear that fly out of the radio,” as Mary Gaitskill wrote in a classic essay for Details, “streamlined by Axl’s high, carnal, glandularly defined voice, is an invitation to step into an electrical stream of pure aggression.”

And the chorus of this song is anger plus righteousness: holy indignation. They’re out to get meee! / They won’t catch meee! / I’m fuckin’ innocent. Who was out to get Axl? Cops. Accountants. “You know,” he expanded in a record-company press kit, “parents, teachers, preachers … everybody.” So the innocence here lives on the underside of paranoia: It’s a dark American innocence, a kind of moral immunity. Not: I’ve done nothing wrong. More like: Nothing I do is wrong. Axl, in this song, is literally unimpeachable.

At some shows, there’s a thrilling sensation of addition: You can feel the room, the crowd, the universe, your brain warping and adjusting to make space for a genuinely new thing. That’s what happened the first time I saw Sleater-Kinney, 30-odd years ago at the Black Cat in Washington, D.C. The music was recognizably in the tradition of post-punk. But the vocals—the rippling vehemence of Corin Tucker, and the unpredictable reactions-in-song of Carrie Brownstein, not a dialogue so much as the bifurcation of an interior monologue—they were something else. The combined effect was simultaneously one of white-knuckle control and an almost voluptuous abandonment.

The singer of this song is someone at the end of her tether, someone who feels like quitting, someone about to incinerate a relationship just to smell the brimstone. Dull as it is to characterize Sleater-Kinney as an all-female trio (no one ever described ZZ Top as an all-male trio), this is music made by women, and the dual action of the women’s voices becomes a way of cutting into experience. All the bridges gonna burn / Gonna fall down / Burn it down, it’s so hot, it’s so hot, hot. It has the rhythm of anguished sleep-talk, of something exquisitely private being said out loud.

Ego: You’ve gotta have one, especially in America. Otherwise, the invisible flying brickbats will take you out. But what happens when ego is not enough—when your loud, repeated assertions of selfhood bring diminishing returns? In 1990, LL Cool J was a former hip-hop prodigy, now a hip-hop superstar, but he was going out of style. His kind of rapping, based in a tradition of boasts and put-downs that stretches back beyond the blues, was being superannuated by gangsta rap, politically conscious rap, basically any rap that wasn’t about the everlasting amazingness of LL Cool J. Still only 22, LL was looking old.

Did the force field of ego flicker? It did not. It redoubled in strength. It swelled with a mighty vibration. I’m gonna take this itty-bitty world by storm / And I’m just getting warm. In this song, over a scorchingly treated loop from James Brown’s “Funky Drummer,” LL spews threats, lands punch lines, and shares visions, expanding to such clanking self-magnitude that the rest of rap music is temporarily blotted out. A hallucination of personal greatness, becoming—while the song lasts—a fact.

To hear that grave voice humorously aroused, that rich, austere voice in a register of levity—it’s like someone has found a joke in the Book of Ecclesiastes. Johnny Cash apparently sprang this number on his band at the last minute, and you can hear them chugging along watchfully behind him, taking their cues from the lifts and the falls and the chuckles in his recitation.

In this performance, three entities are creatively converging. First, the composer: that brilliant cosmopolitan Shel Silverstein, Playboy cartoonist, children’s author, hit songwriter, and—for the duration of “A Boy Named Sue”—cowboy poet, like Robert W. Service with a ’60s glint in his eye. Second, the singer: Cash, with his biblical marrow and his dark glow of charm, a ruefully commanding presence. Third, the audience: the incarcerated men of San Quentin, starved of entertainment, starved of love, aggressively ready to laugh, roar, feel.

Johnny Cash liked playing prisons. He had a connection with men doing time: He knew it, and they knew it. He believed in redemption. (They might not have been so sure.) And this song that he sings them at San Quentin, semi-serious but very serious, is about fathers and sons, and fighting, and becoming a man in America. You can hear it: Inside the prison walls, every punch line, every witty Silverstein rhyme, lands like a revelation.

Suicide: You were either for them or against them. They were a Lower Manhattan art shock, a dividing line—Alan Vega’s phantom voice; Martin Rev’s distorted post-tuneful keyboard blast, like a melted robot trying to remember rockabilly music. Politically, they came out of anti–Vietnam War protests; culturally, they twitched and scurried in the fiscal necropolis that was early-’70s New York City.

Bruce Springsteen was for them. Infatuated with the first Suicide album, he would soon be making Vega-like noises, those atavistic little hoots and yips, on Nebraska. But where Springsteen seemed to be testing the depth of his own isolation, Suicide was into the void itself, an infinite recession of burning skulls. “Ghost Rider”—inspired by the Marvel character, a motorcycle stuntman riding paths of hellfire—is the song of an American demon, nothing but glamour and nihilistic propulsion. Vega gibbers and swoons over a filthy, driving three-note electronic riff: America, America is killin’ its youth. What can you do but follow this trail of incineration across the sky?

A mad professor disguised as a thick-bodied, black-hatted rhythm-and-blues man, Bo Diddley built his own guitars (they were square-shaped), and he built his own rhythms, which were the syncopated thunder of industrial U.S.A., the grating of machine parts, the thrust and clatter that would turn the blues into rock and roll. This song, seething with shakers and maracas, features his signature beat, the Bo Diddley beat—bomp, bomp, bomp, ba-bomp-BOMP—but sped up, with the swing crushed out of it, the better to display the wild moods of his guitar. Diddley was also a trailblazer in his use of the tremolo pedal, and you can hear that going on too: No longer an elegant after-flutter of sound, tremolo in his music was a crude force, driving, destabilizing, its signals overlapping, creating a rhythm and almost uncreating it in the same instant. American volatility, American innovation, American electrification.

Has America gotten crazier in the 15 years since this leering, shuddering, articulated beast of a song was released? Or is it just that the craziness has broken the surface? In their desperate prime, Sacramento’s Death Grips seemed to have cornered the market on free-roaming insanity. Public-transport mutterings, cell-block din, oracular street rants, profane telepathic zaps, hissed rebuttals to the unheard voice: All were gleefully enfolded into their punky-clunky emergency hip-hop. For these guys, in Martin Amis’s phrase, every straw was the last straw. And they could make it catchy.

Across layers of vanilla-smooth pop-jazz, the guitar of Sonny Sharrock comes creeping. Lithe, ductile, unsettling, glimmering with distortion. Something elemental is going on here, a confluence or collision of energies: The flute of bandleader Herbie Mann is charged with breath, whimsically fluttering human breath; Sharrock’s guitar is charged with hulking electricity. There’s something political too. Mann is white, heterodox but commercially oriented, a purveyor in this context of lightweight fluty whiteness; Sharrock is Black, a ferocious improviser and noisemaker—the fumes of the New York free-jazz scene are still on him—who liked, in his own words, to “shatter the tune.”

And how they depend on each other, how beautifully it works, Mann’s little pointillistic puffs against Sharrock’s ragged current. When the guitarist opens up, everything around him—the tinkling vibraphone, the choogling drums—shifts, levitates, and begins to diffuse at its edges into a kind of blinding solar frazzle. The wildness is contained; the container is renewed. America, land of great imbalances—why can’t you do this more often?

Hidden away inside ’80s L.A. hardcore punk, on a track so singular, it’s almost a novelty record, is one of the all-time great American monologues: ludicrous and desperate, solipsistic and righteous, a system-indicting suburban teenage mind-purge. Our narrator, Holden Caulfield with a skateboard, is having problems. He’s thinking about everything, and he’s thinking about nothing. His parents are worried, but they don’t understand. All he wants is a Pepsi, and his mom won’t give it to him. To look at, the members of Venice, California’s Suicidal Tendencies were not theater kids: They were gang-affiliated bruisers, and their shows were famously violent. But what a reading their front man, Mike Muir, gives here, hoarse with pain and thwarted entitlement. This is 1980s American suburbia: Adolescence is being pathologized, and the culture of therapy has a totalitarian shadow. They’re going to put him away.

There’s a flavor of Lewis Carroll about Bert Kalmar’s lyrics here, a pipe-y whiff of old-school English nonsense: For months before my son was born / I used to yell from night ’til morn / “Whatever it is, I’m against it!” This, however, is American nonsense—bigger, shaggier, crazier. (And more Jewish.) Like its English cousin, it depends, for its proper discharge, on order. Authority figures, traditions, uniforms, syntax, meter: It needs the shibboleths of reason to present themselves for destruction. But only America, unchained immigrant America, could have produced Groucho Marx.

Look at him in this scene, at the beginning of Horse Feathers. He is, for some reason, the president of Huxley College, solemnly robed, and the tassel on his mortarboard flips and twitches in a kind of organic irony as he addresses the college trustees. Then he’s away, singing his song of total opposition, American contrarianism raised to a pitch of absurdity, because Groucho would be against contrarianism itself. And it’s not satire either, as Lee Siegel explains in his seriously instructive Groucho Marx: The Comedy of Existence, because even the most violent satire implicitly takes a moral position: For Groucho, there is simply no satisfactory position at all. It’s Bartleby—“I would prefer not to”—on crystal meth.

God

It’s 1998, and Madonna’s club children are weary. The dance floor has drained and deranged them. They have reached the end of the night. So like a balm upon their parched receptors, direct from her all-mothering spirit, she flowingly bestows it: Ray of Light, and its beautiful title track. Mysticism, yoga, breath control. Healing beats. An infusion of wellness before anybody knows what “wellness” is. How many absolute bangers use imagery from the Kabbalah? Not many. How often can we connect a pop song with the Jewish mystical concept of the kav—God’s primal bolt of illumination into the darkness? And this song is a ray of light. The sweetly climbing guitar figure; the soul-elevating groove. Madonna’s voice—that tight, glassy, airless, unmistakable pop-ruling voice—is transformed. Now she roams, now she soars. The great American artist can do this, mass-market the revelation, make the mainstream gleam with the first radiance of the universe.

Fall in love, and you fall in love with everything: Love for another will open your heart to the lovable otherness of the world. Is that the philosophical proposal of this song? I think it kind of is. Through wafts of pedal-steel guitar, she rises, the Texan country-pop queen Kacey Musgraves, floating with cartoon buoyancy past magic mushrooms and luminescent fish toward the you to whom the song is addressed.

The obvious forebear here is “What a Wonderful World,” from 1967, Louis Armstrong’s rumbling beatification of everyday life. But the universe has deepened in weirdness since then. A more contemporary parallel might be Insane Clown Posse’s much-mocked but to me quite valuable “Miracles,” from 2009: Fucking rainbows, after it rains / There’s enough miracles here to blow your brains. “Oh, What a World” is much sleeker and lovelier than ICP, but it partakes of the same—what shall we call it?—experiential openness. Which is an American style of perception, an American freshness: everything shining, everything renewed.

What do you do if you’re a washed-up Beach Boy in 1977? If you’re Dennis, best-looking and most doomed of the Wilson brothers, you pull it all together—all the years of pain and knowledge and queasy close harmonies—and you make a solo record: Pacific Ocean Blue, of which this song is the opener.

“River Song” is immense: a hair-raising, gospel-boosted thumper, proceeding at a gorgeous orchestral trudge, about the river that runs under us all, under all beauty and under all ugliness, bearing us along and carrying us away. Dennis the surfer, his voice roughened by time and substances, has drifted inland—into the veins of the country. (The song came to him in the High Sierras.) The city has used him up; the river beckons. Maybe it’ll do for him what it did for Huck Finn—cleanse the grease spots from his mind.

When John Coltrane died, in 1967, his second wife and musical partner, Alice Coltrane, sought consolation in the presence of the guru Swami Satchidananda Saraswati, part of the second wave of Indian yogis to bring their teachings to the United States. “Anyone listening to this selection,” she wrote in the liner notes to Journey in Satchidananda, of which this song is the title track, “should try to envision himself floating on an ocean of Satchinandaji’s love.”

It’s a busy place, the ocean of love: full of music. Spiny, ego-unwinding tamboura, keen as a sitar; Pharoah Sanders on saxophone, following the line of his breath; Coltrane’s harp. A classical pianist mentored into jazz by Bud Powell, in Paris, she had taken up this instrument only a few years before, and uses it here to put us all into a state of tingling harmonic awareness. Meditation and yoga have arrived in the culture. Listen closely, and you can hear America’s third eye as it flickers its lid, stutters, and then bangs wide open.

Nothing is more American than a personal experience of Jesus Christ. And nothing is more American than getting high. So we need not look for irony here, or any level of sacrilegious naughtiness: Noah Cyrus—sister of Miley, daughter of Billy Ray—and her writing partner PJ Harding are offering this beautiful song to us with the glossy-eyed sincerity of the super-stoned, and the bony earnestness of the spiritually tweaked. Put away your metaphors. They really did get high, and they really did see Jesus, and this is really what he said.

You just need me in your heart / Tennessee whiskey and love: Is this how Jesus talks? I’d like to think so. I’d like to think he has no scruples around derangement, chemical or otherwise—that he’ll show himself to the out-of-their-minds as readily as he’ll show himself to the sober. The music is devotional Americana, slo-mo but not sad, rootsy but with up-to-the-minute production. There’s so much Kingdom left to come: What a line.

The spirit of William Blake visited Allen Ginsberg in 1948, in his cold-water flat in New York. Ginsberg heard Blake’s voice, and Blakean visions of eternity beamed themselves derangingly into his noggin. This is the American mid-century: into the great buildings of the metropolis, a shaft of eternity. Ginsberg’s world was rocked, and his poetic calling was crystallized. In 1958, he wrote up the experience in “The Lion for Real”—not an act of bombastic self-exposure like 1955’s “Howl,” the nervous-breakdown-in-verse that made him famous, but a bumptious, generous, wonderfully slapstick account of the losing of his American mind. This version, recorded more than 30 years after the poem’s composition, finds Ginsberg extra jolly, extra goofy, a kind of outpatient raconteur riding waves of broken jazz. William Blake has become the Lion, a complex golden presence that will neither eat the poet nor leave his front room. What does the Lion want? It wants what America wants: It wants you to face your own nature, your own mortality, your own disgrace, your own divinity.

Who says Jim Morrison wasn’t a great American poet? At first flash of Eden / We raced down to the sea / Standing there on freedom’s shore. What a vista: pristine, Emersonian, the dew-dazzle of original America. But this is 1970. The ’60s are over almost before they began, their great project incomplete. Consciousness remains unredeemed. And Morrison is a broken prophet: heavy, boozy, whiskery. He sounds bemused: This is the strangest life I’ve ever known. The following year, he’ll be dead.

He can still sing, though—that croon of his, Bing Crosby with shamanic antlers. He can lift his voice in a wolfish shout too. The flower children have followed him into the darkness of Freud and Dionysus—weakened as he is, can he lead them now into the virgin dawn? It doesn’t look like it. The people are gathered on the beach, but the sun won’t rise, and the high priest sings his song over a long, withdrawing tide of American serotonin.

Kali Malone is known for the drone. (I can’t help these rhymes.) And the drone goes on forever, but breath is finite. So listen carefully, after each long velvety curving-in-space note played by the ensemble in “No Sun to Burn,” for the discreet sound of a musician inhaling. An American composer based in Stockholm and Paris, Malone works with pipe organs, synthesizers, and—here—brass. “No Sun to Burn” is elegiac in its mood and countercultural in its slowness. The notes accrete, more of a formation than a sequence: It’s like watching a Civil War band being turned to stone while it plays “Woodman, Spare That Tree.” Can it cure your ADD? Your terminal fidgets? Probably not. But listening to it puts you into a different kind of American time. Whatever you’re doing, when this comes on, you’re going to have to stop: stop rushing, stop judging, stop arguing.

Wild American beauty: Iggy Pop in 1973. Big night-creature eyes and the body of an acrobat—like David, if Michelangelo had sculpted him with a welding torch. Like David if he came from a Michigan trailer park. Iggy’s career, however, was in the dumps. Even the tiny constituency of rock-and-roll recidivists that he’d earned as fans with the first couple of Stooges albums seemed to have lost interest. No one appreciated him.

No one? Not quite no one. David Bowie, the parasite genius, the man with the waving antennae and the sci-fi taste buds, had battened on to Iggy. Wrangling him and his band into the studio in London, Bowie mixed Raw Power as a thin scream of sound, a narrow infernal transmission. “Shake Appeal” was Iggy’s favorite track: the closest he ever came, as he later expressed, to being Little Richard. It is indeed shudderingly pure and very danceable rock and roll: The Stooges guitarist James Williamson obliges with a primal solo, a sequence of shrieking but cleanly phrased Chuck Berry–isms. The incoming generation of upstarts would idolize Iggy as the Godfather of Punk, but here he’s nothing more or less than an electrically enhanced child of ’50s America: chest-baring, goofily intrepid, rock-and-roll-adoring, whooping it up, bouncing into the future with Looney Tunes resilience.

The massed voices of the Youth for Christ Choir, from the South Side of Chicago, are at moments in this song almost too seraphically strident: They scrape at the underside of heaven. But what a contrast they offer, what a celestial counterpoint, to the worldly, funky, individual, all-too-human, and very much down-here-with-us voice of Pastor T. L. Barrett, to his ecstasy of personal fallibility. I search for pleasure / But I found pain. Are you listening, young people? This is America’s great and constant sermon: By all means, gratify yourself, but in the end, it won’t be enough. You’re going to need community, and—unspoken in this song, but present in the vertical noise of the choir—a dose of grace from above.

entries.title: The Pinball President
entries.summary: No commander in chief has been better at seizing public attention than Donald Trump. But there is a difference between getting attention and doing something with it.
entries.content:
No commander in chief has been better at seizing public attention than Donald Trump. But there is a difference between getting attention and doing something with it.

In 1946, the year that Donald Trump was born, the pinball machine offered everything but control. The bumpers were propulsive, the lights flashed, but the player’s only honest move was to pull a spring-loaded plunger. After that, the ball belonged to the machine, zinging and zooming wherever the bumpers sent it.

This is how many Americans experience the Trump presidency today: antic caroming that they can do little more than watch. The ballroom. The Iran war. The threats against Canada. Greenland. Portraits of himself as Christ, a decorated general, or the pope. The arch. The Kennedy Center. Prosecution of enemies. Pardons. Imaginary Reflecting Pool vandals. Federal incursions into voting. Tariffs on. Tariffs off. Tariffs on again. The Qatari plane. Endless promises—to release tax returns, to end corruption, to deliver $5,000 checks—that never materialize.

No president has been more with us than Trump, because no president has been better at seizing public attention. But there is a difference between getting attention and doing something with it. For months, the president has been unable to convince the public that he’s up to the job. In a CNN poll released at the end of July, 65 percent of respondents said that his policies had worsened the economy, and only 28 percent approved of his handling of Iran.

Voters have watched the caroming and have concluded that he doesn’t have his eye on the ball. They care about the economy, and he seems to care about everything else. Only 27 percent of adults told CNN that Trump has the right priorities, down from 45 percent when the term began. And a record 73 percent said he hasn’t paid enough attention to the country’s most important issues. In June, while Trump was fixated on the Reflecting Pool and stopping widespread voter fraud that doesn’t exist, a bipartisan housing bill aimed at high costs reached his desk. He called it “a big yawn” and said he hadn’t decided whether to sign it. In July, he let it become law without his signature.

This is a problem for Republicans in November 2026, but it’s an opportunity for voters looking to November 2028. Once a roster of candidates emerges, their supporters will discover that the office demands—wouldn’t you know it?—exactly the qualities that their preferred candidate happens to possess. Now, when there’s no one horse to back, is the time to use the current president’s rat-a-tat treatment of our attention to ask how we want the next president to spend it.

Many voters will ask only one thing of the next president: Don’t be Donald Trump. Fair enough. But stopping at “not Trump” wastes the extremity of the Trump years. Extremes clarify. A flood shows you where the ground was always low.

The Trump years have been a reminder that the presidency is a trust. The public’s attention belongs to the public. A president borrows it, and the test at every turn is whether he spends it on their account or his own. Trump treats it as a possession, to do with as he pleases, like the East Wing. For him, the public is his cheering section. A president who ignores the half of the country that voted against him teaches them that elections are conquests. They will remember that when they win.

It’s true that when Trump wants to focus the nation’s attention on something, he is relentless: immigration, his enemies, his ballroom. In April, The Washington Post found that he had publicly mentioned the ballroom on roughly a third of the days by that point in the year; he had posted about it more than about tariffs. But what he cares about often isn’t in the nation’s greater interest. A trustee doesn’t spend the trust on himself.

The next president should ration his calls on the public’s attention, which, after all, protects his own effectiveness and the country’s. “Public psychology,” Franklin Roosevelt wrote in 1935 to a reporter urging him to speak out more often, “cannot, because of human weakness, be attuned for long periods of time to a constant repetition of the highest note in the scale.” When Roosevelt did speak, he explained. In his first fireside chat, he walked the country through how a bank works. Explanation is what lets a president speak less: A public that has been shown why can carry the argument on its own, and a public that has only been told what must be told again tomorrow.

A president cannot push opinion where it doesn’t want to go, only nudge it, and that is possible only if he hasn’t already worn the audience out. A president who is always talking cannot use talking to signal that this time matters. The creed of this current era is the opposite. “If you’re not making news, you’re not governing,” wrote former Representative Matt Gaetz, who made news nearly every day he served and governed not at all.

A president who consumes the country’s attention spends down a resource that citizens need for their own affairs, including those delightful corners of human experience that should be free of political consideration. The UFC fighter Bryce Mitchell understood this before the bouts on the White House lawn this summer. Mitchell, who did not participate, said that the government was “desecrating its role in society.” The government, he said, “is supposed to protect us, not entertain us.”

Sometimes a president doesn’t have to ask for the country’s attention, because catastrophe has already gathered it. In these cases, a president can act as a moral force, particularly in consolation. Reagan after the Challenger explosion, Clinton after the Oklahoma City bombing, the younger Bush after the attacks of 9/11, and Obama at Emanuel AME in Charleston, South Carolina. Each president spent the nation’s attention on its grief and, in doing so, reminded the nation what it valued. Trump has nearly erased this part of the job, inventing a new one in its place: chief grave dancer. When Rob Reiner was murdered in December, Trump blamed Reiner himself; when Robert Mueller died in March, Trump wrote, “Good, I’m glad he’s dead.”

A president sends a moral signal not just in the words he uses but also in what he chooses to spend them on. After the white-nationalist march and the death of Heather Heyer in Charlottesville, Virginia, in August 2017, Trump denounced the Nazis, but the thrust of his attention was aimed elsewhere. He obsessed over the counterprotesters. He praised himself for being the only one brave enough to name what he claimed were the misdeeds of the people opposing the Nazis. “You had a group on one side that was bad, and you had a group on the other side that was also very violent,” he insisted without evidence, “and nobody wants to say it, but I will say it right now.” He sent six tweets about Charlottesville and, in those tweets, never used the terms racism, bigotry, or white nationalism. He sent 37 tweets about NFL players kneeling during the anthem.

All of this happens where we can see it. We tend to treat the presidency as if it existed only in that public form. Most of it doesn’t. Because much of the job happens in secret or out of camera range, what the president chooses to do with public attention is our best evidence of how he sorts the world in private. That evidence has limits. A president who never mentions the deficit might be working on it every morning. Eisenhower’s style was called the “hidden hand”: The president who looked idle at the podium was working the levers out of sight. But a president whose public attention shows no discipline, discernment, or patience isn’t going to discover those attributes at the necessary scale when the cameras turn away. Trump governs by the Heisman hand, always in your face.

The presidency demands brutal prioritization. “I have two kinds of problems, the urgent and the important,” goes a line that Eisenhower liked to quote. “The urgent are not important, and the important are never urgent.” It was such a simple idea that it became the Eisenhower Matrix, used by managers everywhere to sort incoming challenges. The principle applies with more force in a job where the urgent arrives by the hour. If missile stockpiles are low, we want a president fixing that now, not giving a speech about the deficit. But we also want a president who can see the deficit coming and feel some obligation to the future citizens who will live under galactic debt. Trump spends a lot of his time on matters that are neither important nor urgent. The New York Times reporter Maggie Haberman, who has covered Trump for 30 years, has said that if you charted his mind these days, 70 percent of it would go to gilding, construction, renaming, and tribute projects.

The exhaustion after Trump will produce an appetite for quiet. It has happened before. George W. Bush campaigned on restoring dignity to the office because Americans were worn out by the dramas of the Clinton years; he wanted a presidency that his team promised would show up on page A24 of the newspaper. But quiet is not a standard. The office needs a benchmark built from the job itself, not from the last man to hold it. Nor should the next president react to Trump’s frivolity by turning every subject into a family talk in the living room about Important Matters—a brittle standard where partisans adopt the posture of the online scold who answers “I love dogs” with “Your silence on cats is deafening.” Under that standard, a president must speak to everything, and a president who speaks to everything has no time left to do anything.

Campaigns often measure for qualities that have little or nothing to do with the office. But voters can evaluate how candidates treat public attention on the campaign trail and make some inferences about how they would approach the job. Here are some questions to ask: Does the candidate choose problems that a president can actually move, and can he say why those and not others? Can a president articulate a vision for the country to people who are not likely to vote for her? Can he explain rather than merely assert? Does she ever talk about a problem that won’t pay off before the next election? Can he let a news cycle pass without joining it? And when grief or outrage arrives, does he show any evidence of a concern for the entire nation? How a candidate handles these moments during a campaign—when public attention, ever more scarce in the age of the algorithm, is the only thing he has to spend—tells us how that candidate will spend ours.

In 1947, the year after Trump’s birth, pinball changed. The flipper was added, which meant the player was no longer merely watching. Where the ball went was now, at least in part, up to the player. In 2028, voters will be in the game again. But that requires attention to the office now.

entries.title: A Show That Lovingly Pokes Fun at Gen Z
entries.summary: Culture and entertainment recommendations including Adults, Emmylou Harris, and more
entries.content:
Culture and entertainment recommendations including Adults, Emmylou Harris, and more

This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.

Welcome back to The Daily’s Sunday culture edition, in which one Atlantic writer or editor reveals what’s keeping them entertained. Today’s special guest is Emma Williams, an associate editor who helps oversee the magazine’s social media and has also written about her home state of Texas.

Emma is a habitual rewatcher of Normal People, a show that she says has resonated with her differently over time. She also enjoys listening to her namesake Emmylou Harris, laughing over Adults episodes, and watching Hailee Catalano’s comforting cooking videos.

— Stephanie Bai, senior associate editor

The television show I’m most enjoying right now: The first scene of FX’s Adults tells you pretty much everything you need to know about the show: It’s crass, crude, absurd, and indulgently hilarious. Adults pokes fun at Gen Z without being judgmental or predictable, and it features some familiarly ridiculous plights. Maybe don’t watch it with your grandmother—but your spunky aunt is probably okay.

A quiet song that I love: I discovered the British DJ Fred Again when I was going down an NPR Tiny Desk Concert rabbit hole years ago. I was immediately struck by his talent—but over time, I have come to better appreciate the emotion he evokes through his performances. Even in his natural habitat, behind the DJ booth, Fred isn’t what you might normally expect from an EDM artist: He samples spoken-word poems, Zoom calls, and random internet videos to create songs that you can just as easily dance to as you can cry to.

I know I’m cheating a bit by saying that his entire Tiny Desk production is my favorite quiet song, but the fact that he was able to pull off an acoustic EDM performance is remarkable. To re-create the sound of electronic beats, he used the marimba, the vibraphone, and the piano; he also pounded and tapped on a desk and layered in his soft, husky voice. It is gentle, engrossing, and stupidly impressive.



A loud song that I love: The first time I heard “Dance Yrself Clean,” by LCD Soundsystem, I was confused. My best friend played it for me, and by minute two, I was enjoying the song, but I could not comprehend how this hazy and somewhat repetitive tune could continue for another seven minutes and be as “life changing” as she had promised.



Then I hit 3:05 on the track. I felt the ba-da-da-dum in my bones before James Murphy’s newly impassioned voice flooded through the speakers. This is now my song for any moment when I need to drown out my thoughts. Whether I’m going through a breakup, a bad day, or an existential crisis, I’ll put on “Dance Yrself Clean” and itch through the first three minutes, eagerly anticipating the rush of euphoria that hits after the beat drops.



Years later, that same friend and I heard the song live. I have no idea whether we were crying or laughing or shouting, but I know we were dancing with abandon—and letting the music wash over us.

A cultural product I loved as a teenager and still love: I watched Normal People for the first time when I was 19, and I’ve rewatched it at least once a year every year since. I have never wavered in my fondness for it, but my reaction to the characters and storylines has evolved with time.



When I first saw the show, based on Sally Rooney’s novel of the same name, I fell madly in love with Connell, barely registering that his cold avoidance of Marianne in public was wrong. I just thought he was broody and complicated; therefore, to my teenage mind, he was perfect and dreamy. I’m glad to say that I have moved past that (kind of), and I now find it difficult to watch his treatment of Marianne in the first few episodes.



In my 20s, I resonate more with Marianne’s college arc. Specifically, her need to become the coolest, most stylish, most successful version of herself—even if it comes at the cost of her own happiness.



Marianne and Connell’s lack of clear communication is always maddening. But I understand it more with age. Sometimes vocalizing what you really want can be more terrifying than staying quiet.

A musical artist who means a lot to me: I have to pay homage to my namesake, the inimitable country folk artist Emmylou Harris. Her music reminds me of my home state of Texas. Listening to her song “Boulder to Birmingham” transports me back to long drives through the plains of West Texas and the seemingly endless miles of wind turbines. I hear my parents’ voices, lovingly calling me Emmylou and Emmy-lou-lou. Whenever I feel adrift, her music pulls me back to the ground.

A YouTuber, TikToker, Twitch streamer, or other online creator I’m a fan of: I have an embarrassing confession: There is a cooking influencer whom I’m really obsessed with—as in, I went to a meet and greet of hers, and I send her the occasional tipsy Instagram DM. (Sometimes she even responds!)



Hailee Catalano is a James Beard–winning chef. Her food is fresh and unique, and her video style isn’t gimmicky or aggressive like that of so many other cooking accounts—it’s simple and personable. My favorite series of hers is called Friday Night Dinner, which is a collaboration with her partner, Chuck Cruz, who is also a chef and content creator. They film themselves making a new meal every week, and I can only describe their vibe as homey. The videos sometimes have awkward pauses and funny asides (and, of course, clips of their dog, Gus), and watching them makes me feel like I’m sitting at the kitchen counter as two of my friends prepare something delicious for us to eat.

A poem, or line of poetry, that I return to: The older I get, the more I find myself recalling the lines of Langston Hughes’s poem “Harlem.” Hughes asks: “What happens to a dream deferred?” I recently turned 25, and the “quarter-life crisis” is certainly hitting me. I think about all of my childhood hopes that have dissipated, and all of the ones I still have that I’m not sure will come true. I, too, wonder what happens to these dreams.

Here are three Sunday reads from The Atlantic:

The Week Ahead

By Kai Williams

In late July, one of the world’s most famous mathematicians issued a warning to his field. Math is entering a “turbulent period,” the UCLA professor Terence Tao said in front of a packed lecture hall at the International Congress of Mathematicians. AI is getting so good at math, he said, that it’s causing a “crisis in our mathematical values and practices.”

Earlier in the same week that Tao gave his talk at math’s most prestigious conference, a researcher at Anthropic had used Claude to disprove an 87-year-old math conjecture. entries.title: Guatemala’s Democracy Dilemma
entries.summary: A reformist president weighs the pressure to move fast against the imperative to restore institutions his people can trust.
entries.content:
A reformist president weighs the pressure to move fast against the imperative to restore institutions his people can trust.

Just over three years ago in Guatemala, a coalition of young and Indigenous voters helped propel Bernardo Arévalo, a reformer who campaigned against corruption, to an astounding presidential win. Guatemala had not only refused the global trend toward populist authoritarianism; it had also defied what its citizens called “the pact of the corrupt,” a loose alliance of politicians, judges, criminal networks, and crony capitalists that had gained control of the country’s institutions.

Today the mood in Guatemala is less hopeful. Some of Arévalo’s former allies, and many of those who voted for him, are dejected, convinced that the president missed a once-in-a-generation opportunity to transform the country. When I met with Arévalo in Guatemala City in May, he defended the pace of his administration’s progress and suggested that the alternative would have been to abuse the powers of a government he was elected to reform.

In Latin America, “we never truly got used to understanding that the rule of law is fundamental,” he told me. “Rule of law is not the same as rule by law. Rule of law is when we all accept that we are subject to the law and we operate within that framework to solve problems. Rule by law is when I use the law that’s at my disposal as part of my political arsenal.”

Had he crossed that line, Arévalo insisted, he would have risked being ousted by his opponents and replaced by someone willing to do much worse. His critics disagree.

Arévalo’s personal integrity is undisputed. But some of the reformers who helped elect him now argue that he may be too scrupulously rules-respecting to deal effectively with the “pact of the corrupt” and the institutions it captured—too much of a liberal democrat to save democracy. When he leaves office in 2028, they fear that the pact will quickly retake control of the few institutions it has lost, or that voters will choose an autocrat who promises to crush crime without concern for legality.

Guatemala’s predicament points to a more universal problem. Can liberal reformers unwind authoritarian state capture without, themselves, engaging in at least a little bit of illiberalism? The dilemma is not Guatemala’s alone. Move too aggressively, and you risk being branded an autocrat, or even becoming one. Move too cautiously, and you risk obstruction, sabotage, and ineffectuality. South Africa’s Cyril Ramaphosa chose a gradualist approach to reversing Jacob Zuma’s state capture and disappointed many of his supporters. Placing the opposite bet, Poland’s Donald Tusk bent rules to try to undo the damage done by the right-populist Law and Justice party—and stood accused of undermining the rule of law. Hungary’s post-Orbán leader, Péter Magyar, seems to be following Tusk’s example.

In a way, both Arévalo and his critics are right. Guatemala has avoided a democratic breakdown. But the president’s rules-bound approach has also left many Guatemalans feeling that he has not fought for them forcefully enough. The question now is whether Arévalo has preserved democracy as an ideal that Guatemalans believe in and, if necessary, will defend.

In Guatemala City, I watched as hundreds of people gathered outside the country’s public prosecutor’s office, a bunker-like building ringed by a huge black-steel fence put up three years before, allegedly to shield the occupants from nonviolent democracy protesters. The crowd had come to celebrate the long-awaited end to the term of María Consuelo Porras, the country’s attorney general and, to many citizens, the personification of the pact of the corrupt.

For the past eight years, Porras had been a figure of fear. She used the power of her position to investigate and jail critics of state corruption. When Arévalo was elected in 2023, her office tried to overturn the results, alleging irregularities that international observers found baseless. That effort looked likely to succeed—until indigenous Maya communities organized peaceful demonstrations that lasted 106 days and drew the participation of nearly 2 million Guatemalans. Arévalo was inaugurated.

That he did not take extralegal action to remove Porras from her post has given rise to some of the fiercest criticism against him. She opened an investigation into Arévalo’s party, the Seed Movement, for relatively minor party-registration irregularities. Although the probe did not produce formal charges, it led to the party’s dissolution and thus thwarted any hope of its controlling Congress. Porras also brought more than 75 legal cases or complaints against the president and his supporters, including the arrests of two of the Indigenous leaders behind the 2023 protests, and even a cabinet minister. Now Porras was finally leaving, and a new attorney general was taking over.

The Guatemalans gathered outside the office had waited for this moment. What they had not anticipated was how long Porras’s departure would take, and how few people would come out to celebrate it. Thousands had massed in the same street just a few years before.

When I met Arévalo a few days later, he justified the delay by explaining that his government had arrived “with an enormous level of public legitimacy, but without control of the Congress, and with the justice system positioned against us.”

Legally, he had no authority to simply eject the attorney general. He sent a bill to Congress to grant him that power, but the opposition blocked it. “If, in that scenario, I make a political miscalculation, the result isn’t that I go with a hundred people to pull Consuelo Porras out of that building and that this is sustainable and produces results,” he said. It was that “I go to prison or into exile, and someone else comes in, one of them, to take power.”

Like much else in Guatemala, the colossal, mint-green presidential palace where Arévalo sat down with me is a holdover from a bygone era of authoritarianism. It was built by Guatemala’s Hitler-admiring, yet U.S.-backed dictator, Jorge Ubico, who rose to power in 1931 and was forced to resign amid mass protests in 1944.

Arévalo, before winning the presidency, was best known as the son of the man who succeeded Ubico, in Guatemala’s first truly free elections. Juan José Arévalo, an educator and a social democrat, returned to Guatemala from exile in 1944 to run for president against the ex-dictator’s favored candidate. As his son would later, he won by a landslide, and Guatemala’s “democratic spring” began, a time of expanded rights and education. But after his freely and fairly elected successor, Jacobo Arbenz, went further, carrying out a land reform that threatened the interests of wealthy families and the powerful U.S.-based United Fruit Company, the United States organized a coup that put the military in power in 1954. Nine years later, a guerrilla leader asked Arévalo to help spearhead armed resistance to the regime, and the former president refused, saying that confronting the military head-on would turn Guatemala “into a lake of blood.”

He was right. In the name of crushing the greatly outnumbered guerrillas, the military and its allies killed or disappeared more than 100,000 Guatemalans over the next three decades. It massacred leftists, labor leaders, and residents of more than 400 Maya villages suspected of supporting insurgents. Guatemalan courts eventually deemed the latter crime a genocide.

Bernardo Arévalo, born in exile in Uruguay, returned with his family in the middle of the dictatorship period, and he began a career as a diplomat at its tail end, as the country formally returned to elections and civilian rule in 1985. He later left the diplomatic service, earned a Ph.D., and worked in international peace-building.

The wood-paneled presidential office where we met was decorated only with two portraits: his father’s, in black-and-white, and his own, beside it, in color. Arévalo’s demeanor was professorial.

“We are in a process of recovery,” he said. “Democracy doesn’t develop in a linear, unidirectional way; it has leaps and twists, not only here, but everywhere in the world.” For much of the 1990s and 2000s, Guatemala had been twisting its way toward democracy, but corruption networks and drug traffickers had insinuated themselves into the country’s institutions. “Part of what we set out to do is to recognize the serious damage this had caused the country—this corrosion, this penetration of political-criminal networks” that served no “ideological interest,” Arévalo said, but rather “the highest bidder: whoever could pay for impunity.”

Dislodging these forces from the machinery of the state has been neither swift nor straightforward, and even those most anxious for change are hard-pressed to offer practical solutions. The president told me that some supporters had asked him to use the military to remove Porras. He found the suggestion unsettling: “Are you really asking us to go back to the years of military dictatorships of the 1970s, when armies were the only solution?”

I asked Arévalo about the Indigenous protest leaders, Luis Pacheco and Hector Chaclán, who had then been imprisoned for more than a year while under investigation on terrorism charges. “I would like the people who say ‘But the government could have done something else’ to tell me what,” Arévalo replied, exasperated. “What they’re venting is the frustration we all feel.”

He assured me that the pact of the corrupt was weakening incrementally as its networks lost access to the state: first the executive branch, then the public-works contracting system, now the prosecutor’s office. “Without tools, they aren’t powerful. And our task is to keep removing those tools from them.”

Arévalo can point to some successes. Young lawyers have worked to clean up corruption in the judicial selection process. Appointed in March, the new bench of the  Constitutional Court, which rules on the constitutionality of laws and policies, is more favorable to reformers than the one it replaced, as is the new electoral tribunal, which oversees elections. I spoke with the new attorney general a few days after he assumed his post: He was so busy firing Porras’s apparatchiks and preparing for the institution to resume serious criminal investigations that he was sleeping only four or five hours a night. An anti-corruption commission that Arévalo formed early on has already filed more than 200 criminal complaints against former officials.

Arévalo was tasked with not only freeing a state captured by kleptocrats, but also strengthening one that was fundamentally weak. The bureaucracy he inherited had little capacity to provide public services, reduce poverty, or fight organized crime. In this, too, his administration has made some progress. It has hired more than 15,000 new teachers, and built or refurbished more than 150 rural-health clinics (his predecessor built just six in four years, Arévalo said). The government has also replaced dirt floors with cement in more than 75,000 households in the country’s poorest rural municipalities, and has distributed water filters and cleaner-burning stoves.

Still, much else that Guatemalans had hoped for has failed to materialize. Congress, which remains dominated by the old-guard pact forces, has blocked or stalled bills aimed at curbing corruption—for example, bills to modernize public-works contracting, require shell companies to disclose who owns them, and protect whistleblowers. Partly because the contracting system remains dysfunctional, the government has made little visible progress toward repairing the country’s crumbling highways. And, unwilling to buy votes in Congress outright, as his predecessors did, Arévalo has resorted to pork-barrel spending and raising congressional salaries to win legislative support. Such tactics are deeply unpopular with the public.

Another limiting factor has been the Trump administration. Although Arévalo’s cooperation on crime and drugs has kept the relationship cordial, his opponents have courted President Trump to try to tip the scales against reformers. In April, the U.S. ambassador to Guatemala personally called reluctant Guatemalan lawmakers to pressure them to approve a Constitutional Court judge favored by pact elites and conservatives, a top lawmaker, Luis Aguirre, told me. This tied the court between reformers and their opponents, leaving Arévalo without a reliable majority.

The young reformers who campaigned with Arévalo knew that he would face constraints, but some wish that he had more often tested those limits.

Samuel Pérez, 34, is a member of Congress; he was also the head of the Seed Movement bloc in Congress before it was dissolved. I went to see him in a building plastered with missing-persons flyers for those who were disappeared during the military dictatorship decades ago. The flyers are a common sight in Guatemala City, posted and reposted by the victims’ families.

Pérez told me that Arévalo was elected not only “to overthrow the regime, but also to construct something new, and that isn’t happening.” Now Pérez was creating a party, called Raíces, to which most of the lawmakers formerly associated with the Seed Movement had defected. They would still support Arévalo, but they would advocate for a more confrontational approach. “The president interprets power and good government as doing things a little better and a little more than what already existed. For me, no. You don’t use power to administrate what’s already there, but to transform what isn’t working,” Pérez explained.

I’d last seen Pérez during Arévalo’s presidential campaign in 2023. He’d told me then that if the Seed Movement won, the government’s greatest difficulty would be managing popular expectations. But he hadn’t predicted that he himself would be among the disappointed. Arévalo should have rallied the public to pressure Congress to pass the law removing Porras, Pérez said. He should have conceded less to business elites, and done more to free Pacheco and Chaclán. Pérez was particularly upset that the police had come to arrest the two men in a white van with tinted windows—a symbol of the dictatorship, which used such vehicles to disappear its victims—and that the government had not stopped this.

Several young Guatemalans in the reform movement suggested to me that the political caution of their parents’ generation was a product of the fear instilled in them during the years of military rule and internal armed conflict. Some speculated that Arévalo’s aversion to escalation emanates from that experience, too, given his youth in exile and the persecution of many of his father’s supporters in the years after the 1954 coup. “I think he is a son of his circumstances,” said Andrea Reyes, a young lawmaker helping Raíces organize.

Arévalo readily locates his most formative influences in that era—as a source not of fear, but of strengthened conviction. He spoke to me of his father’s refusal to abandon democratic principles: “Even when the world began to change around him, he kept his convictions, which today we see were the correct convictions, after all, 80 years later.”

Arévalo, too, has found his convictions under pressure—not only from former allies who worry that his reforms have gone too slowly, but also from constituents and conservative politicians who want a government that will ignore constitutional limits in cracking down on crime. In this they compare him unfavorably with the autocrat next door: Many Guatemalans who live in daily fear of extortion and kidnapping see gangs, not illiberal state capture, as the biggest threat to their basic freedoms, and they see President Nayib Bukele’s El Salvador as a beacon of safety.

Bukele, first elected in 2019, took an almost opposite approach from Arévalo’s to governing. He purged institutions of his political rivals, packed them with loyalists, and then cut secret deals with gang leaders before cracking down on their followers. His mass roundups virtually eliminated violent crime in his country, by jailing more than 90,000 people suspected of gang ties, many without due process. Arévalo is unwilling to pursue such methods. He has, however, seized record quantities of cocaine, extradited crime bosses, hired thousands of new police officers, and begun building the country’s first new maximum-security prison in 40 years. But murder and extortion rates have proved stubborn, and many are now demanding more-radical methods.

“Guatemalans are searching for their Bukele,” said Alvaro Arzú Escobar, a conservative lawmaker sanctioned by the Biden administration for allegedly trying to undermine Arévalo’s inauguration. Arévalo “isn’t radical in his ideas or his actions,” Arzú told me. But, he added, “the country’s biggest problem right now is a lack of authority. As president, he doesn’t exercise the power he holds. There is a lot of rhetoric, but little action.”

The Mariscal Zavala military prison sits on a pine-covered ridge on the outskirts of Guatemala City. A former army base, it houses the state’s highest-profile prisoners. I went there to meet Pacheco and Chaclán, the Indigenous leaders who’d played such an instrumental role in safeguarding the 2023 presidential election. Both had been on the board of the 48 Cantones of Totonicapán—one of the country’s oldest Indigenous self-governing bodies, in rural western Guatemala—when the attorney general’s office had moved to annul the vote. Pacheco and Chaclán canvassed rural villages on foot, helping gather some 50,000 signatures calling for Porras’s resignation. Later they helped organize protests in the capital.

“The 48 Cantones is also a democracy, with elected leaders and term limits,” Chaclán told me. “For us, democracy is sacred, and although Guatemala often doesn’t reflect it much, we must respect it.”

In April 2025, Porras ordered him and Pacheco into pretrial detention. After that, their court hearings were repeatedly delayed, seemingly intentionally, and when I met them in May, they had no idea when the next one would be.

I asked them whether they believed Arévalo should have rallied protesters or found some other tool to remove Porras, and thus to free them. Pacheco responded, “I would have liked it at first, but later I realized it would have only changed the person, not the form of doing justice.” Chaclán added, “This is nothing simple, and surely he is doing what is best for the country. We have faith we have already passed the majority of our time here.”

Chaclán was right. On August 5, a judge released Pacheco and Chaclán to house arrest, reuniting them with their families. Around the same time, the prison-like, black-steel fence was taken down from around the public prosecutor’s office.

Guatemala’s next presidential election is just nine months away. Right-wing candidates are beginning to emerge, some imitating Bukele, and many sure to court the White House, in the hope that Trump will try to tip the scales. Arévalo’s and Pérez’s reformists claim that they will join forces behind a unity candidate, but such a figure has not yet surfaced. Democracy is twisting its way forward, in Arévalo’s words. No one thinks it is leaping.

But the passage of time may provide a different perspective. On one of my last days in Guatemala City, I walked by a cathedral I had passed dozens of times before. I had never previously noticed the tiny engraved names of more than 13,000 victims of the internal armed conflict, so small as to be illegible from even a short distance, on its stone columns.

For much of the 20th century, Guatemalans who advocated for self-government, equality before the law, and the welfare of the majority—that is, social democrats—knew that the state might try to kill them. Today, social democrats govern. Reformers may disagree as to whether Bernardo Arévalo made the most of the opportunity he was given. But that such an opportunity could ever arise is more than many members of his father’s generation likely thought possible.

*Image Sources: Luis Soto / AP; Johan Ordonez / AFP / Getty; Arnulfo Franco / AFP / Getty.

entries.title: 190 Days Without a Homicide
entries.summary: How a record stretch of peace ended in my hometown.
entries.content:
Jenee Gragston dropped to the ground and held on to the grass as if it could save her life. She yelled to her family members to get down. She later told me that she didn’t know where the bullets were coming from, but she knew they were close. When the firing stopped, the cries began. She could hear her 4-year-old nephew howling: “Get it off me! Get it off me!” She wasn’t close enough to see what had happened, but it looked like he had blood on his chest. A teenage boy was lying near the child. The teenager “never screamed or anything,” she said. “I can still see all of it.”

It was a Saturday afternoon, mid-August in Lexington, Kentucky. Hundreds of people had gathered in Charles Young Park to celebrate what’s called East End Day—a combination of family reunions, live music, and lots of food. I grew up going to festivals in that park, though I lived on the west side of town, in the Charlotte Court housing projects.

Kentucky isn’t the most dangerous place in America, but it’s up there, with the 14th-highest rate of gun deaths. Twelve years ago, my uncle was murdered in Lexington. Three years ago, my sister’s husband was shot and killed there. I worry about my brother, who still lives there. He had gotten himself off the streets for a while, but is now back living in the city. Lexington had recently seen a hard-won drop in gun deaths—last year was the fourth straight year of declines in gun violence among young people. This spring and summer set a record of 190 straight days without a homicide. Then came the East End Day shooting, which killed that teenager, 16-year-old Di’Zhon Robertson, and wounded four others—including the 4-year-old, who was shot in the leg. The next weekend, another person was killed. The weekend after that, four separate shootings left two more dead.

Gragston was selling Polish sausages in the park. She’d paid more than $300 for the grill, $300 for the sausages, more than $1,000 in fees, $75 for the booth. Business was good; some people returned for seconds. Her husband, her kids, and other family members had come to help her set up her tent. Her 4-year-old nephew was handing customers sodas and water bottles. On the basketball court nearby, Devine Carama was talking with a group of young people. Carama is the director of ONE Lexington, a city-funded program that tries to prevent gun violence by mentoring at-risk boys. He, too, threw himself down when he heard gunfire. “I almost got shot that day,” he told me. Two people near him were hit—a man and his girlfriend. Carama and others tried to bandage the man’s leg; he told me he could see a glimmer of bullet or bone through the blood.

A day later, 18-year-old Jametrius Griffin turned himself in and was charged with murder. According to court testimony, Griffin’s younger brother had gotten into an argument; punches were thrown, and the younger brother fell or was pushed. When Griffin saw that, he yanked out a gun and started firing.

For the past three years, Robertson had participated in ONE Lexington’s summer youth program, which offers workshops on building emotional and social skills, as well as college-campus visits. “He wasn’t a street kid,” Carama said. Griffin’s younger brother was in ONE Lexington, too—in its school mentoring program. The organization had also helped Griffin get a job at UPS. The group’s work seemed to be making a difference. And then a fight left one young man dead, one wounded, and one in prison.

In many ways, Lexington feels like a small town, where everyone knows everyone. I went to middle school with Griffin’s lawyer, Daniel Whitley, who has a big reputation locally for representing people accused of murder—and for winning their cases. The week after the shooting, I spoke with Whitley and with Griffin’s mother, Jay-Me Baxter, on a video call.

“A bunch of bullshit” was how Baxter described the park shooting, “because everybody’s friends and everybody’s family.” She said her youngest son told her he had been bullied by Di’Zhon Robertson and others. The day after the shooting, she made the same argument in a video she posted on Facebook that outraged many in the community. She suggested that her older son had had no choice and said she didn’t care “who makes it home as long as mine do.” (I tried to reach Robertson’s mother through family members to see if she would talk with me about what happened to her son; her sister replied that the family didn’t want to relive it. But friends and family members described the teenager as quiet, observant, and “very respectful.”)

“I’m like, Shit, I know Di’Zhon’s mama,’” Baxter told me—the other mother was close friends with her own sister. Baxter said she had had a conversation with her about the beef between the boys, and assumed the issue had been settled. Griffin loved football, and he had started college at Kentucky State University. “But you know them kids,” she said. “They be doing stuff in silence.” Her son must have been simmering with fury.

I knew Baxter’s family growing up—she’s a year older than me, and they, too, lived in the Charlotte Court housing projects. She didn’t remember me, but she knew my brother. Her mother was white, and had nine children. Baxter, the third-oldest, is half Black, like her younger siblings. But the oldest two are white. Her mother used to cry, Baxter told me, because “the white kids didn’t ever live with us.” In our majority-Black neighborhood, a white mother with mixed-race kids stood out. Baxter remembers people throwing rocks through their windows and a lot of name-calling—“white bitch.” Her family was poorer than many others, but people in the neighborhood assumed that she was privileged, and tormented her for it. “That white mama, man,” she said. “You know what I’m saying?”

That kind of bullying is part of the pain of being impoverished. You feel so low, you desperately want to make someone else feel lower.

Baxter is a single mother, and Griffin is the oldest of her five children. Like my own mother, she lost custody of her kids because of drugs—she signed over her parental rights to her mom. She told me the story as if she was discussing a character in a book: “Jay-Me got in trouble. Jay-Me started using drugs, cocaine specifically.” Like my mother, Baxter was a victim of sexual abuse. She grew up watching her mother “get beat by men. I done been touched by men, and I never told my mama until a couple months before she died.”

It took Baxter seven years to stop using drugs and get her kids back. Those kids needed her, yet she kept choosing drugs over them, she said, as her voice cracked and tears hit her cheeks. “That hurts, because I can’t believe I did that.” I’ve heard those same words from my own mother and watched her cry for the same reason.

Before Baxter signed over her rights, she said, she asked her mother to promise that what she’d experienced as a little girl wouldn’t happen to her kids. She wanted to break the cycle of violence, poverty, and dysfunction that is the inheritance of so many children. “I’m not a gun mama,” Baxter told me, but she believes in “stepping in the street” to fight. “I’ve been fighting all my life,” she said.

Backgrounds like these are so common in Whitley’s line of work that he seemed to tune out our conversation. At one point on the video call, we heard the sound of snoring. Baxter joked about it: “Listen to him. My lawyer tiiiiiired.” We continued talking for a few more minutes and never heard from him again. “Night night, Daniel,” she said before we hung up. He called me back later, apologized for not saying goodbye, and said he hadn’t been asleep.
